name: Tonsillectomy

card.summary: Surgical removal of the tonsils, discussed in looksmaxxing as a last-resort fix for severe tonsil stones and breath odour; guidelines support it for recurrent infection and sleep apnoea, not for stones.
card.note: Major surgery under general anaesthetic; bleeding and prolonged pain are documented, and Wikipedia reports no good evidence for using it for tonsil stones or bad breath.

quick.overview:
A tonsillectomy removes the palatine tonsils from the sides of the throat. It is among the most common operations in children, and guidelines recommend it for frequent, well-documented throat infections and for sleep-disordered breathing caused by enlarged tonsils.

In looksmaxxing and bad-breath discussions it is raised as a permanent answer to severe tonsil stones. Medical sources describe it as an option clinicians may consider when persistent bad breath from tonsil crypts does not respond to lesser measures, but they also state that good evidence for that use is lacking.
quick.mechanism: With the tonsils gone, the crypts where stones and debris collect no longer exist. The surgery is done under general anaesthetic using dissection, electrocautery, coblation or similar tools, and recovery takes one to two weeks.
quick.risks: Bleeding is the most common serious complication, occurring in roughly 0.2 to 3.3 percent depending on timing. Throat pain is substantial, especially in adults, and deaths, while rare, are reported. Other risks include dehydration, nausea and anaesthetic complications.

lead: For some people, tonsillectomy is a route to fresher breath and a more comfortable, confident mouth: the operation removes the tonsils where tonsil stones and recurrent infection collect, and people with persistent stone-related bad breath sometimes consider it after other measures have not helped. Where enlarged tonsils obstruct breathing, removal can also change how a person breathes and sleeps, which is why it appears in discussions of mouth breathing and facial development.[2][19]

Tonsillectomy is the surgical removal of both palatine tonsils, usually under general anaesthesia. It is one of the most frequently performed operations in children, and in the United States remains the second most common outpatient surgery in that age group; the main indications are recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.[1][2][5]

In looksmaxxing and halitosis communities it is mentioned as a definitive option for severe tonsil stones (tonsilloliths), since the stones form in the tonsil crypts. Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence for tonsillectomy as a treatment for tonsil stones or bad breath in children [2], while a general reference on tonsil stones lists partial or complete tonsillectomy at the end of a ladder of options that may be considered if bad breath persists [3]. Dental-hygiene and ENT sources describe a surge of tonsil-stone content on TikTok from about 2021, and clinicians have reported both unnecessary home-removal injuries and a rise in patients asking about surgery.[17][18]
Published guidelines emphasise selective use, because many sore throats resolve without surgery and the operation carries bleeding and pain risks.[4][5][6]

chain: Tonsils removed, so the crypts that trap debris no longer exist
Stone-related bad breath and recurrent throat infection no longer arise from those tonsils
Fresher breath and fewer sore-throat flare-ups
angle.text: People with persistent tonsil stones who have not responded to rinsing, irrigation or crypt-smoothing procedures sometimes consider tonsillectomy as a permanent way to remove the source of the stones. In children with enlarged tonsils, removal is also discussed for its effect on nasal breathing and facial growth.

infobox: About 7 to 10 days (full recovery 1 to 2 weeks)
Tonsil removal; adenotonsillectomy when combined with adenoid removal
Saltwater gargling, oral irrigator, curettage, laser cryptolysis

paras: The palatine tonsils are paired lymphoid tissue masses at the back of the throat. A tonsillectomy removes them completely, in contrast with tonsillotomy (intracapsular reduction), which removes most of the tissue and leaves a thin layer. Adenoids are often removed in the same operation, called adenotonsillectomy.[2]

Surgeons use several techniques: cold dissection with a scalpel, electrocautery (roughly 400 degrees C), coblation (plasma at about 40-70 degrees C), harmonic scalpel, thermal welding and laser methods. Reported bleeding and pain outcomes between techniques are conflicting, and registered trials have compared coblation with cold dissection, monopolar electrocautery with cold dissection, and intracapsular approaches in adults.[2][9][10][11]

Wikipedia lists recurrent or chronic tonsillitis and sleep apnoea as the main indications, with peritonsillar abscess, PFAPA syndrome and tonsil cancer among others.[2] The Paradise criteria, derived from trials in the 1980s, set frequency thresholds, such as seven documented episodes in one year, five a year for two years or three a year for three years, for recommending surgery in children.[2] The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery issued clinical practice guidelines for tonsillectomy in children in 2011 and updated them in 2019; the update says there is no clear preponderance of benefit over harm even for children meeting the criteria, so surgery or watchful waiting are both reasonable and shared decision-making is advised.[5][6][2]

For obstructive sleep apnoea, a sleep study is advised to confirm the diagnosis, and a paediatric guideline covers diagnosis and management of childhood obstructive sleep apnoea.[12][2] A 1998 study linked sleep-disordered breathing to poorer school performance in children.[13]

Wikipedia reports that a 2018 UK analysis of records for 1.6 million children estimated that about 90 percent of the roughly 37,000 children undergoing the operation each year were unlikely to benefit under evidence-based criteria.[2] A 1982 comparison of New England, England and Norway documented wide regional variation in how often the operation is performed, and later data show several-fold differences between regions of England and Germany.[14][2]

Tonsil stones are mineralised debris in the crevices of the tonsils; Wikipedia says up to about 10 percent of people have them, many without symptoms, with bad breath the most common sign and others reporting a foreign-body sensation, sore throat or cough.[3] The stones contain a biofilm with layered aerobic and anaerobic bacteria that produce volatile sulfur compounds, the compounds associated with halitosis.[3] A 2007 study found stones in 75 percent of patients with bad breath and 6 percent of people with normal breath readings, and a 2009 study found biofilms inside the stones.[3] Dental-hygiene literature describes them as most common in adults in their 20s to 40s and less common in children, whose crypts are shallower.[17]

The tonsillolith article lists options in rising order of invasiveness: no treatment if the stones cause no problem, saltwater gargling and gentle manual removal, a low-pressure oral irrigator, antiseptic rinses such as chlorhexidine, curettage or CO2 laser cryptolysis to smooth the crypts, and tonsillectomy when bad breath persists despite other measures.[3] Wikipedia's tonsillectomy article states that evidence for tonsillectomy for stones or bad breath is lacking in children.[2] Dental-hygiene guidance says tonsillectomy may be considered for large or recurrent stones.[17] Published research on tonsillectomy done specifically for stone-related halitosis consists mainly of observational series rather than randomised trials.

Children with enlarged tonsils and adenoids often breathe through the mouth, and orthodontic literature has long associated chronic mouth breathing with a more vertical facial pattern, a retruded lower jaw and a narrower upper jaw. A 2012 prospective study in the Brazilian Journal of Otorhinolaryngology followed 53 children aged 6 to 12: 33 with obstructive tonsil and adenoid hypertrophy and 20 controls, using cephalometric measurements before surgery and at 14 months.[19] Before surgery the obstructed children showed a more vertical growth pattern, retruded mandible and narrower maxilla than controls. After adenotonsillectomy they showed significant changes in vertical, sagittal and width measurements, and the authors concluded that surgery improved facial growth, with the effect more evident when combined with rapid maxillary expansion.[19] The authors point to differences in how the control group was described between abstract and methods, so the comparison is read with care.[19]

Other small studies reach varying conclusions, and no large randomised trial has examined whether removing tonsils changes adult facial structure. The topic connects to online discussion of mouth breathing, jaw posture and "mewing", although the surgical literature is about children with obstruction rather than cosmetic outcomes.

For recurrent throat infection in children, a summary of Cochrane evidence reports about 0.6 fewer sore throats in the following year, with benefits not lasting long and many children improving without surgery.[2] One review of five randomised trials reported episodes dropping from 3.6 to 3.0 per year.[2] For sleep apnoea, surgery improves quality of life and symptoms in most children, though a 2015 Cochrane review found no benefit for attention or school performance, while another review found school improvements.[2]

For adults with frequent tonsillitis, the 2023 NATTINA trial in the UK, published in The Lancet, found tonsillectomy more effective and cost-effective than conservative management, with fewer sore-throat days.[2] A 2025 randomised trial has examined tonsillectomy for adult obstructive sleep apnoea.[2] Registered trials of intracapsular tonsillectomy in adults are ongoing or completed.[11][15]

Throat pain typically lasts about two weeks and is generally greater in adults than in children; a large 2013 cohort study of 179 operations included tonsillectomy among procedures producing high first-day pain.[2][7] Full recovery is commonly described as 7 to 10 days to two weeks, with a soft diet advised by some surgeons.[2] Ibuprofen and paracetamol are recommended for pain, and codeine is not recommended under age 12.[2] The scab over the tonsil bed sloughs at roughly 7 to 11 days, the period when secondary bleeding most often occurs.[2]

Bleeding is the most common serious complication, with primary bleeding in the first 24 hours reported in 0.2 to 2.2 percent and secondary bleeding, typically 7 to 11 days after surgery, in 0.1 to 3.3 percent; risk is higher in adults.[2] Delayed discharge occurs in about 1.3 percent and readmission in up to 3.9 percent.[2] Reported death rates range from about 1 in 2,360 to 1 in 56,000 procedures, roughly a third from bleeding.[2] Other risks include nausea, dehydration, ear pain, taste changes, dental or airway injury and anaesthetic risks.[2]

Wikipedia reports no evidence of long-term immune impairment, but cites meta-analyses reporting associations between tonsillectomy and later inflammatory bowel disease, with odds ratios of about 1.9 for Crohn's disease and 1.2 for ulcerative colitis in a 2024 analysis; an umbrella review of environmental risk factors for IBD is among the published literature on the question.[2][8] Associations with other conditions have also been reported, with varying strength of evidence.[2]

Wikipedia traces tonsil removal to descriptions by Celsus around 50 AD using a finger and blunt hook, with Galen advocating a snare and Aetius in the late fifth century recommending partial removal to limit bleeding.[2] Philip Syng Physick modified an instrument of Benjamin Bell into the tonsil guillotine in 1828, which was standard for more than 80 years, and Ballenger's 1897 work favouring complete removal displaced it in the United States.[2] By the 1930s the operation was very common; in 1934, 61 percent of 1,000 New York schoolchildren had undergone it.[2] Studies from the 1940s to 1970s linked surgery to bulbar poliomyelitis, and a 1950 paper addressed the question.[2] US rates fell after a 1978 NIH review found insufficient evidence of benefit, and UK rates declined in the 1970s after studies reported limited effectiveness.[2] In 2006 the UK Chief Medical Officer estimated unnecessary tonsillectomies and hysterectomies cost the NHS about 21 million pounds a year.[2]

sections.h: In looksmaxxing culture and social media
paras: Tonsil stones are discussed in oral-health, breath and general looksmaxxing spaces as a cause of persistent bad breath that brushing does not resolve. A study by Sulibhavi and Isaacson of Temple University, reported in Ear, Nose and Throat Journal and summarised by ENT Today, described a clinic seeing growing numbers of mostly female and teenage patients presenting with stones and linked the pattern to TikTok videos of intraoral selfies and do-it-yourself removal methods; they reported home remedies leading to injury and unnecessary surgery.[18] A later study by Bharat and colleagues, summarised in a dental-hygiene journal, found that from 2016 to 2021 patient visits for tonsil stones and tonsillectomies increased alongside removal videos; the summary stresses that this is an association and not proof of cause.[17]

Dental-hygiene guidance cautions that videos can exaggerate severity and show unsafe tool use, and that DIY removal can cause infection, bleeding, scarring, gagging and choking; it advises that professionals handle removal and that hygienists promote oral hygiene and refer to dentists or ENTs when needed.[17]

Evidence includes clinical practice guidelines in 2011 and 2019 for tonsillectomy in children [5][6], a technical report on childhood obstructive sleep apnoea [12], a 1998 study linking sleep-disordered breathing to poorer school performance in children [13], and the NATTINA trial in adults.[2] A prospective cephalometric study has examined facial growth after adenotonsillectomy.[19] No controlled study found specifically tests tonsillectomy as a treatment for tonsil-stone-related breath odour.
Registered trials include intracapsular tonsillectomy for sleep apnoea and recurrent tonsillitis in adults and a trial of tonsillectomy and IgA nephropathy outcomes.[11][15][16]

timeline.event: Celsus describes tonsil removal by finger and hook.[2]
Philip Syng Physick introduces the tonsil guillotine, standard for over 80 years.[2]
Ballenger advocates complete removal, displacing the guillotine in America.[2]
61 percent of 1,000 New York schoolchildren have had tonsillectomy.[2]
NIH review finds insufficient evidence of benefit; US rates decline.[2]
NEJM compares surgical rates in New England, England and Norway and documents wide variation.[14]
AAO-HNS publishes its first clinical practice guideline on tonsillectomy in children.[5]
Brazilian cephalometric study examines facial growth 14 months after adenotonsillectomy.[19]
UK analysis of 1.6 million children estimates most operations fall outside evidence-based criteria.[2]
AAO-HNS updates its guideline; no clear preponderance of benefit over harm even when Paradise criteria are met.[6][2]
Temple University clinicians describe TikTok tonsil-stone content and patient presentations.[18]

lore.intro: Tonsil stones are widely discussed on social media and in breath-focused communities, and tonsillectomy is mentioned as a permanent endpoint when other measures have not helped.[17][18]

claims.claim: Removing the tonsils permanently ends tonsil stones and the bad breath they cause
claims.believers: Patients and social-media posters describe tonsillectomy as the only way to remove the crypts where stones form.[17]
claims.experts: Dental and ENT sources list tonsillectomy as an option when halitosis persists despite other measures, but Wikipedia states that evidence for tonsillectomy for stones or bad breath is lacking, and no controlled trial has tested it for that purpose.[3][2][17]

claims.claim: Stones should be removed at home with picks, swabs or water jets
claims.believers: Videos on TikTok show teens removing stones with household tools.[18]
claims.experts: Temple clinicians reported injuries and unnecessary surgery from home remedies, and dental-hygiene guidance lists infection, bleeding, scarring and choking among risks.[18][17] Saltwater gargling and low-pressure irrigators are listed as gentler options.[3]

claims.claim: Tonsil stones are always a sign of poor hygiene
claims.believers: Some posters treat stones as a hygiene failure.[17]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that up to about 10 percent of people have stones and many have no symptoms; dental sources describe a bacterial biofilm in the crypts and note deeper crypts in adults.[3][17]

claims.claim: Tonsillectomy is a quick procedure with a short recovery
claims.believers: Some social posts describe it as a minor fix.[17]
claims.experts: Recovery is typically 7 to 14 days, pain is generally greater in adults, and bleeding occurs in roughly 0.2 to 3.3 percent depending on timing.[2][7]

claims.claim: Removing enlarged tonsils and adenoids can improve facial growth in mouth-breathing children
claims.believers: Orthodontic and mouth-breathing discussions connect nasal obstruction to a longer, narrower face.[19]
claims.experts: A 2012 prospective study of 53 children reported significant facial-growth changes after adenotonsillectomy, more evident with maxillary expansion, while noting that surgery alone does not correct anatomic changes.[19]

claims.claim: Tonsillectomy is routine and nearly always warranted when throats are sore often
claims.believers: Parents and patients often expect surgery after repeated sore throats.[2]
claims.experts: The 2019 guideline says surgery and watchful waiting are both reasonable even for children meeting the Paradise criteria, and a UK analysis estimated about 90 percent of operations fell outside evidence-based criteria; in adults NATTINA found surgery more effective than conservative care.[6][2]
